title: The boy at the door
hookLine: Parvati shapes a son from earth and breathes life into him; why families welcome Ganesha into clay
carry: the holy can live in clay
tomorrow: the boy says no to the next one at the door. who is it?
last: YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO ACT. NOT TO THE FRUIT.

lines: NOBODY IN THE HOUSE IS HERS.
cards: Parvati lives with Shiva on Mount Kailash, and every guard at the door is one of his ganas, his attendants, loyal to him. Whenever Shiva wants in, they step aside. Nobody in that house is simply hers.
So before her bath she takes the paste she rubbed on her skin, the earth of her own body, and shapes a boy. Then she breathes life into him. The first face he ever sees is his mother's.
She hands him a staff and gives him one job: guard this door. No one comes in.

teach.b: That boy grows up to be Ganesha, the god you met on day one. This telling is the Shiva Purana's, a collection of stories about Shiva, and it isn't the only version. Notice what he's made of.
Not thunder, not light. Earth, shaped by the Goddess's hands, with her breath in it. Hindu homes still act this story out.

teach.h: GANESH CHATURTHI: A GOD OF CLAY.
teach.b: Every year at Ganesh Chaturthi, many families bring home a Ganesha shaped from clay.

teach.h: PRANA PRATISHTHA: SETTING THE BREATH IN.
teach.b: With prayers they invite him to live in it, a rite called prana pratishtha: setting the breath in. For a few days he's the guest of honor, fed, sung to, visited by the whole street.

Then they carry him to a river or the sea, and give the clay back to the water. The teaching under it: God can be welcomed into something as ordinary as earth, and loved there, without being trapped there.

teach.h: THE HOLY CAN LIVE IN CLAY.
teach.b: That's one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: God isn't only far off in the sky. God can be found in what's right in front of you, even a handful of earth. And somewhere down the mountain, someone very large is walking home.

how: At Ganesh Chaturthi many families bring home a clay Ganesha, invite him in with prana pratishtha, and after a day and a half to ten days immerse the image in water (visarjan). His birth story is often retold then.

s: Ganesha was born with an elephant's head
in this telling he starts as an ordinary boy, shaped from earth. the elephant comes later in the story.
at Ganesh Chaturthi, the clay Ganesha is kept forever
most families give him back to the water after a few days. that's visarjan.
there is only one version of Ganesha's birth
the story comes in more than one version; the Shiva Purana's is the one told here.

games.q: a friend asks: if you put the clay Ganesha in the ocean, was he ever really god? what fits today's teaching?
o: for many Hindus, the clay was his home for a while. he isn't lost when it goes back to the water.
no, it was only ever decoration.
yes, so the clay should never be put in the water.
games.why: families invite Ganesha in with prayer and later bid him farewell. the image is holy for a time; letting it go doesn't let God go.

practice: For two minutes, pick up something ordinary near you that matters to you: a ring, a mug, a photo. Hold it. Notice that it's just stuff, and also not.
Something you love has been breathed into it. Then set it down gently. It's still yours.

wordCard.voice: Ganas: Shiva's attendants, the guards of his house. Keep an eye on them. The boy made of earth is going to end up leading them.

orig.note: Sanskrit: lord (isha) of the ganas, the attendants. The boy at the door grows into their leader.

carryVoice: Your line: the holy can live in clay. Parvati shaped hers from earth. See you tomorrow.
